disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more non-bizarre or plausible-sounding delusions lasting at least one month, in the relative absence of other psychotic features such as prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or marked negative symptoms. Outside of the delusional beliefs, cognitive functioning and behavior are often largely preserved, and overall functioning may remain relatively intact compared with schizophrenia. The content of the delusions can be persecutory, somatic, grandiose, jealous, or erotomanic, and individuals often come to clinical attention because of interpersonal conflict, occupational problems, or legal/organizational involvement stemming from their fixed beliefs. The course tends to be chronic, with limited insight and resistance to contrary evidence, distinguishing it from overvalued ideas or mood-congruent beliefs seen in major mood disorders.

narrative.stressor: About a year before presentation, Barrington was assigned to lead a high-visibility safety compliance initiative after a minor collision on one of the county bus routes drew local media scrutiny. Around that time, a contentious interaction with a senior driver—who openly questioned his authority in front of others—seemed to linger with him, and he began poring obsessively over inspection logs and incident reports, convinced that someone within the department was deliberately undermining his work. Over the following months, his belief that a small group of colleagues and outside contractors were secretly targeting his inspections hardened, leading him to stay late documenting minor issues, confront supervisors about perceived plots, and avoid certain routes and drivers when organizing trainings, even though his basic job performance remained technically adequate. The situation came to clinical attention when his supervisor, concerned about increasingly tense staff meetings and reports from church friends that he was "taking work way too personally," referred him to the employee assistance program, where his fixed, highly elaborated belief about being sabotaged became apparent.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m here because no matter what anyone says, I know some people at work are secretly working together to set me up, and nobody seems to take that seriously.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly a year before seeking help, Thanh went through a period of intense stress when her mother developed complications from diabetes, leading Thanh to accompany her to multiple specialist visits and spend long hours in medical settings outside her own clinic job. During this time, she became preoccupied with the idea that certain patients and staff at her high-volume clinic were being selectively exposed to experimental pathogens under the guise of routine bloodwork, initially framed in her mind as a far-fetched but plausible ethical concern. As months passed, this belief became more rigid and elaborate: she started meticulously tracking which patients were sent to which labs, altered her volunteering at community health fairs to "warn" certain groups, and significantly increased her own health-related rituals and avoidance of specific colleagues, yet she continued to function at work well enough that supervisors only saw her as "overly intense." Her family finally urged psychiatric evaluation after she insisted on moving her mother’s care to a distant hospital to avoid a perceived research network and became visibly distressed when relatives and coworkers challenged her firm conviction that a hidden research program was targeting Vietnamese patients.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m convinced some labs are secretly using people like my mom and our community in dangerous experiments, and no one can show me anything that truly proves otherwise.”

narrative.stressor: About a year ago, after his second unsuccessful attempt at securing a major research grant and watching a younger colleague get a coveted faculty position, Coleman began to fixate on the idea that a small group in his department’s grant review committee had decided to block his career advancement. Initially, this surfaced as frustrated comments about academic politics during late-night brewing sessions and hikes, but over time the conviction solidified: he started attributing minor scheduling changes, delayed email replies, and neutral feedback on his teaching to a coordinated effort to sideline him. Despite continuing to perform adequately as a teaching assistant and maintaining his hobbies, he increasingly withdrew from departmental social events, avoided certain collaborators, and spent long evenings combing through funding announcements and committee rosters trying to "prove" the pattern he saw. His spouse eventually persuaded him to see a psychiatrist after he refused an offer to co-author a paper—insisting it was a trap to discredit him—and came home from a faculty meeting visibly upset that "everyone was pretending" not to acknowledge the supposed conspiracy.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I know a few people in my department have quietly agreed to block my grants and promotions, and I can’t shake that belief no matter how much my wife or colleagues argue with me.”
